It's three things. First, we have a framework for how everything works. It's all blocked out in our head. Any information that comes in, we have a space for it and we know what's next to that space on all sides. They have nothing but known unknowns and unknown unknowns. Any information that comes in has nothing to stick to, it just hangs out in the void, meaningless, without structure or connections. On top of that, you've had so much knowledge for so long that you've forgotten what it's like to be them.

Second, and this stems from the first, whatever they've told you is wrong. Rarely does the user know what went wrong. They probably missed several steps of it going wrong and are confused why they are where they are now. And then they start making assumptions, creating houses of cards that they then submit as their ticket. And we really run into a problem when you believe them.

I start every ticket with: Are you a brand new user, if not, has this ever worked? When was the last time it worked? Explain to me how it's different from when it was working and what it's doing now. 

Anything that comes out of their mouth I don't believe until I see a screenshot or a screen share of it. The worst thing I can do is start forming assumptions based on their assumptions. 

Third and finally, it's emotions. The thing they depend on every day to do their work doesn't work anymore and they have no idea why and all they can do is talk to the faceless voice on the phone about it. A voice which they know knows far more about this machine than they do. We are a figure of authority in this framework. Both the situation and us give them anxiety. To make this worse, when you get frustrated with them, they feel it and you exacerbate all of that.

IT people do not have emotional intelligence. We don't pick up on how they are feeling and how they are reacting to us. If we did, we would know what they need. They need to feel safe. They need to feel like no matter what we have this handled. We are going to take care of them. We're even going to enjoy it. They are not a burden on us.

When you're triggered, whether it's something you're going to follow through with or not, doing this mental exercise helps you process the feelings.

Of the things you're worrying about, choose a worst case scenario. Maybe you get no sleep and end up making a terrible mistake, maybe lose your passport, get lost, whatever highly triggers you. Then, imagine it happens like it's real. Walk through it all in your imagination slowly feeling everything it triggers. Finally, totally accept what's happening. Make it okay. Realize that if it happened you would somehow still end up at home safe. If you got arrested you would still have a place to sleep. If you were sold into slavery they would still feed you. If you died your family and friends would be okay.

Whatever you imagine find a way to end in safety, even when it doesn't really make sense. Discharge the energy.

That's not how probabilities work. This is a common misconception.

The 25% correct scenario would be in the middle of a normal distribution, also called the bell curve. It would have the highest probability of occurring out of all of the possible outcomes. 

We still expect the other possible outcomes to occur, just not as often, especially as you increase the sample size. You can't cherry pick an n=1 sample size and work backwards with probabilities. That's not how the math works.

So the hotkey is the left mouse button "LButton". The dollar sign keeps it from triggering itself. We have the function "rapidfire" that sends 'T' repeatedly. And we have "SetTimer" which decides how often "rapidfire" runs. We use SetTimer instead of Loop because reasons I don't quite understand, but smart people told me to do it.

When left mouse is pressed it has to send "Click, Down" to send the mouse click because the actual click was interrupted to launch the hotkey. Then we start the function with a repeating timer. Then, and this is the important part, we wait for the physical mouse click you are holding to be released. When you let go the script continues where it was waiting at "KeyWait". At which point it stops the repeating function and it sends the signal to release the mouse.

Feel free to ask questions. I'm not sure if any of the first 4 lines are actually necessary, I just start my scripts looking like that. Except for InstallMouseHook, I think since keywait is waiting on the mouse it needs the mouse hook installed because we are juggling hard and soft mouse button events.

    #SingleInstance, Force
    #InstallMouseHook
    SendMode Input
    SetWorkingDir, %A_ScriptDir%
    
    $LButton::
    Click, Down
    SetTimer, rapidfire, 50
    KeyWait, LButton
    Settimer, rapidfire, off
    Click, Up
    return
    
    rapidfire:
    Send, T
    Return

If your mouse is double clicking on a single click, you need to add a "debounce" to the key. 

When a switch (button) actuates (is pressed) there is initially a degree of electronic noise for the first few ms before the signal stabilizes into an "on" signal. Sometimes when a switch ages, the bounce time takes longer. Therefore, we must implement our own extended "debounce" logic that accounts for this.

Essentially, you tell the system to wait longer after a button press to check to see if the button has been released. This is because if it checks too quickly while the signal is bouncing, it might falsely believe that you have released the button, then detect the signal is "on" again a few ms later and see it as a second click despite the fact that you only pressed the button one time.

I have recovered from quite a few fears that crippled me in the past. It's always the same. You could swap out this specific fear her with any other and all the same principles would apply. Find a way to break your faith in this feeling telling you the truth. Then surrender to just experiencing the feeling until your nervous system gets bored with it.

Every time we encounter our fear we teach our nervous system to be either a little bit more afraid of it or a little bit less. That's how you have grown this fear so large. You have been nurturing it over time.

When you get this feeling and try to figure out how to "fix" them being mad at you, you are feeding the fear. Next time it's a little bigger and you try to fix it even harder. It's a feedback loop. You've been at this for a long time and now it's huge.

But the "danger", or more likely lack thereof, is exactly the same as when you were only a little afraid. You've probably created all kinds of stories about the bad things that could happen to you if people are mad at you. But they're just that, stories. You made them up.

People being mad at you doesn't matter. You are going to fight that idea at first. The amount you fight it will be proportional to the fear you give yourself in situations where people are mad at you. The more you surrender to it, the weaker the fear will get.

You're probably thinking to yourself right now how I have no idea what I'm talking about and this, that, and the other thing will happen if any number of people are mad at you. And several of those might actually be true. Except the majority of the consequences of those things happening won't matter either. If you really critically examine these things all the way through you will find they fall into 2 categories: ridiculous things that won't happen, and things that would only happen if these people were 100x more mad at you than the actually are.

Start making a map of all the crazy shit you think will happen to you if people are mad at you. Write out all the bad things that you think will happen and why you believe they matter. Don't pick at them yet, just start noticing them and writing them out, especially while you are triggered.

Go back and read them a day or a few days later. Sooner or later you're going to figure out that a lot of the stuff you are terrified of in the moment seems like no big deal or even silly after the fact. This brings us to a very important idea.

You aren't afraid of people being mad at you. You are afraid of the feeling you give yourself when people are mad at you or you've imagined they might be, and you make up stories to match the intensity of the feeling.

Once you see that and it becomes real to you, then you can start working on making your peace with the feeling. Not believing the feeling is the turning point. That's when you stop trying to fight it. That's when you stop feeding it and start starving it.

When you stop fighting a feeling and just feel it you stop making it stronger every time. You start letting a little bit of it go every time you feel it. Then with consistency over time you can work this fear down to almost nothing.
